Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I stated when I first rose, I have just returned from western Canada, where I found a very serious situation with respect to farm
Farm Implements

machinery for harvesting our present crop.
I interviewed a large number of farm machine agents while out there, and found that practically all of them have orders for from one to twenty pieces of farm equipment which they cannot supply at the present time. This is a serious situation in view of the fact that we have a prospective crop of approximately 450,000,000 bushels of wheat coming forward in western Canada-wheat that is urgently needed throughout the whole world.
This situation has arisen because of certain actions of this government. We have heard a lot of discussion of the causes of this serious shortage. We have heard members of the government say and have read in the press throughout Canada that this farm machinery shortage is the result of a shortage of steel, a shortage of pig iron, and various other causes. But in my opinion these are not the real reasons for the present shortage. As I started to say when you called me to order, Mr. Speaker, the shortage is owing mainly to the policy of the government in having during the year 1945 issued export and reexport permits for 20-2 million dollars' worth of Canada's total production of 46-4 million dollars' worth of farm machinery during that year, and having during the first six months of 1946 issued export permits for $16,382,400 worth of farm machinery, and having during the first five months of 1946 issued export permits for $4,319,626 worth of reaper-threshers, of which $2,395,318 worth have been exported to the United States, in consequence of which the present serious situation exists.
Some four weeks ago I received a letter from a returned man in my constituency. While serving overseas for four years his father died and left him a section of land, which he returned to farm. He stated in his letter that he wanted nothing from the government, that all he wanted was the opportunity to buy sufficient farm equipment to do a proper job on that land. He needed a new plough, and asked me if I could get for him a priority for the purchase of it. I was unable to do so. The only thing he could do was to take a loan from the Veterans Land Act administration, thereby obtaining a priority. He did that, but the type of plough he wanted was not available. He wanted a larger type of implement than the Veterans Land Act administration had available for him.
In spite of the fact that this machinery was not available to this veteran we exported from Canada in the first five months in 1945 $2,251,960 worth of disc ploughs, ploughs and plough parts, to the following countries: Belgium, Costa Rica, French Africa, Greece,

Mexico, Morocco, Peru, Dominican Republic, Eire, United Kingdom, Syria, British East Africa, British South Africa, Southern Rhodesia, British India, British Guiana, Jamaica, British West Indies, Newfoundland, Australia, New Zealand-it sounds like a lesson in geography-Argentina, Belgian Congo, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Mexico, The Netherlands, Paraguay, Poland, San Salvador, Santa Domingo, Sweden, Turkey, Uruguay, Venezuela, Yugoslavia, and the United States. Yet we could not supply our own returned men, who have been overseas fighting for this country for the last four years, with the implements of production when they return to this country. I say that is a serious situation, one which this government should be prepared to face.
Why should the government issue to our machine companies permits to export machinery to every country in the world, or practically every country? As a matter of fact I have the list of exports for 1945, which shows that we exported farm machinery to seventy-one countries. I was alarmed at this situation, and I placed certain questions on the order paper with respect to this matter. Not only that, but I asked on the orders of the day on June 20 of this year-Hansard, page 2659 the following question, which was directed to the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Is the minister aware that there are pools of farm machinery in western Canada and that the machinery is being held and not distributed? Is he aware that this machinery is urgently needed by veterans? In view of the fact that in some cases it is proposed to reship this machinery back to the United States, will the minister make the necessary inquiries and issue the necessary orders to see that this machinery is distributed in Canada and not sent back to the United States?
I received the following answer to my question:
The wartime prices and trade board say that the only "pools" of farm machinery in western Canada are Veterans Land Act pools. No farm machinery is being exported to U.S.A. which can be used in Canada.
Note that sentence.
Export is controlled by the administrator of farm machinery, wartime prices and trade board.
In view of the facts which I have just placed before you, that in reaper, harvesters or combines alone in the first five months of this year we have exported $4,220,14S worth, urgently needed in western Canada, and that we have exported to the United States in that same five months 82,395,318 worth-

irrespective of the needs of the Canadian people. And this applies not only to farm machinery but to a lot of other commodities as well. How is it that through UNRRA 500 Canadian trucks have been given away to Finland, an enemy country, while our farmers need them so badly? This is one thing that struck me. It is that spirit of internationalism, which I have denounced bitterly, that runs everything in this country.
I should like to have the production of trucks under the control of the Minister of Reconstruction, and he should also have the delivery under him so that Canadians would be served before the enemy. The minister is all right, and he alone should have both controls. The consul of a minor country has more influence than all the members of parliament put together in regard to the disposal of our own property.
Canadian citizens have a mortgage on the production of this country; Canadians should be first served, and if something is left over then we shall be able to serve others. We speak about housing; if housing is far behind it is because many men have not the trucks they need to carry lumber to the mills and the manufactured product to the consumer. These trucks are indispensable. We need them very badly, and yet we send them to an enemy country. Then we speak of the sovereignty of Canada; we speak of Canada being an autonomous country. We are run by Stalin, Bevin, Byrnes, Chiang Kai-shek and Bidault. They are the ones who ran the country. I wrote to the private secretary of one of the ministers that when the request is made by a Quebec easterner instead of by someone from Ontario, or even a foreigner the latter has a better chance to get these goods than a Canadian. How is it we have to write so much to get so little? I do not blame the minister; he is not to blame now because he has not the full control of the whole thing and cannot give us the distribution we would have if this government and this parliament had not that silly policy of giving everything to others without keeping anything for ourselves. That is the policy. Members appear to complain about it, but they supported the so-called external policy of this government, which amounts to nothing for us, because all the dominions of the British empire are run from outside; their sovereignty is an illusion.
Canada had nothing to do with the war with Finland except to declare war. We did not send a man there, but we are sending trucks. We were at war with that country because another power was at war with it. We sent trucks which our farmers are crying for, but they do not get anything. That is the way it stands.
I hope that I shall be permitted to say something to my colleagues about the reform which is necessary in this country. Everybody is for reform, but reform in the abstract, which means nothing at all. When we come down to brass tacks it is easy to count the members who make constructive suggestions to improve conditions in Canada. There is a haze which blurs the eyesight of men who should see clearly through the disorder which exists precisely because of the neglect and carelessness of the members of parliament. I regret it, but the trouble is that no distinction is made between what is important and what is not. It is taken for granted that so-called experts are those who should run this country, men who are not responsible to the people, men who are the products of universities and who are ready to teach the world about what is to be done immediately after they get a degree with a gold seal. And here we are. We listen to them just as if no one knew how to read and write, no one could make a sound decision. I ask hon. members to make their own decisions about everything, to consult their own judgments and act accordingly, and the country will be much better run.
Sometimes it is a very small suggestion which may be accepted. But what is swallowed by the whole House of Commons? It is precisely the product of the intelligentsia which all denounce so bitterly as bureaucracy.

All the laws are prepared by bureaucracy. Members may denounce bureaucracy, but they swallow the draft legislation which is prepared for them, without asking any questions. Sometimes they denounce it, but they do not go to the source of the evil.
When I was on the other side of the house I suggested that we should have a union opposition, an opposition composed of all men of good will-and nearly all members are members of good will.

I thank you, sir. What I just said was the preface to my conclusion. My conclusion is that instead of complaining about the state of things which everybody deplores, members of the House of Commons irrespective of party should unite and decide what the majority wants. In this case I suggest that all members of parliament should unite to give full control to the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe). Give him a trial; give him an opportunity to settle the question as well as he can, notwithstanding the steel strike and the other difficulties which confront us. It is precisely because of the domestic difficulties that we have to be indulgent to the minister. We must not blame him for conditions for which he could not be held responsible. The duty of members of parliament, if they really want what they ask for, is to set aside all party considerations and unite to put the business of the country in good shape. In this particular case it would be very easy. Each member would have only to consult his own judgment and make his own decision, and I am sure a large majority of the members would join together and settle this difficult question of the distribution of farm implements, trucks, and even automobiles.
If one spends his time blaming the Minister of Reconstruction for all he has done to improve manufacturing conditions in this country I do not find it fair. I will not say that it has been done for political considerations, but it should be done for a higher political consideration; it should be done to

Farm Implements
improve the lot of those who are in need, and the need can be shown. How is it that it is impossible to secure advice? We get only criticism. There is ground for criticism.

speechtext: The hon. member will not listen to advice.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I always listen to advice which is full of common sense, but I never listen to criticism which is full of bitterness. We have a duty to fulfil; we have a duty to help our fellow citizens, to help them right away instead of wasting our time in useless criticism. There should be constructive criticism in order that there shall be useful suggestions to improve the lot of the farmers of Saskatchewan and of farmers all over the country, particularly the farmers of eastern Quebec. I remind my hon. friends of the prairie provinces that they are not the only ones to suffer. In eastern Canada we suffer as much, and my colleagues of Quebec are as much devoted to the cause of the farmers as my colleagues of Saskatchewan may be to the cause of the farmers in their part of the country. But the time has arrived to do something, and if my hon. friend who interrupted me a moment ago has another constructive suggestion to offer, I shall listen to him with delight. If a suggestion is sensible I shall support it; but I should hope that from the fertile minds of so many hon. members something will come to help out the farmer, and not only the farmer but all those who earn their living with implements of any sort.
It is time for us to make a thorough investigation into what is going on. The war expenditures committee has been sitting for a long time; I have read its reports, but there is no improvement. What has been said by the hon. member who moved this motion shows that the work of the committee has not been either practical or profitable to this country, because now we have a state of affairs about which everyone complains, in spite of the fact that this committee has held numerous sittings and heard numerous witnesses. Therefore all I ask my colleagues to do is to think, to listen to the voice of their conscience and to obey their own natural judgment in coming to decisions that will serve this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: As I said, Mr. Speaker, Canada is a deficit country in regard to farm implements, in that we have always imported far more than we exported and have required far more than we produced. That is just as true to-day as it was in earlier days, in spite of the fact that the production of farm machinery in Canada trebled between 1939 and the present time. In other words our capacity for manufacturing farm machinery is three times as great to-day as it was in 1939. The farm implement industry is operating to capacity and has been for several years, up to the limitation imposed by the recent steel strike. My hon. friend suggests that we could stop exporting entirely, and that other countries would still export to Canada.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
He certainly implied that. I suggest to him that farm machinery is just as short in the United States as it is in Canada, yet the United States is exporting to Canada. Why? Because throughout the war Canada and the United States worked with
Farm Implements

each other on. the basis of equality of sacrifice. That has been the principle on which we have dealt with the United States since the early days of the war. The principle was established at the time of the Hyde Park agreement and has been followed in recent years, I may say very much to the benefit of Canada. Only a few months ago the United States made a move to cut off the export of tractors to Canada; there was a terrific shortage of tractors in the United States. Canada is wholly dependent upon that country for tractors. We immediately went to Washington, raised the principle of equality of sacrifice, and succeeded in having our quota maintained. Could we have done that had we adopted the policy suggested by my hon. friend and kept everything we made in Canada for our own purposes, depriving our foreign customers of the Canadian implements upon which over the years, they have been taught to depend?

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: How much did we get from the Argentine?

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Canada has been a supplier of implements to the Argentine republic for a great many years. I was in that country between 1930 and 1934, and I noted then that Canadian implements had a very large share of that market at that time, as they have had ever since. I do not know that my hon. friend would suggest that we cut off such an historic market under present conditions.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Well, he did suggest that.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Who has been the principal buyer of Canadian farm implements for export in recent years? I can tell my hon. friend that. The principal buyer has been UNRRA. Why has UNRRA been buying? So that it could help solve the food situation in the devastated countries. Why do we ration flour in Canada? Let me ask that. We do it so that we can send food to the devastated countries and help them avert starvation. Well, farm implements are the equivalent of food. All during the war we cut back many items of civilian production, but we did not cut back the production of farm implements; we expanded that production. Why? Because farm implements were implements of war. It was just as important to England during the battle of Britain to obtain farm implements from Canada as it was to obtain food itself, because farm implements meant food. We did maintain our exports of farm implements to the United Kingdom during the war years, and we expanded them as much as we could, in the 
meantime taking care of Canada's most urgent needs. We kept up that traffic during an acute shortage of shipping. Britain gave it the highest priority in shipping, and every effort was made to maintain those shipments as a matter of the highest importance to the people of both countries. We are exporting to the devastated countries to-day, though the proportions of those exports are not as great as in war years. We fully recognize the need to take care of the Canadian market; and let me say that I believe the needs of the Canadian market are satisfied to a higher degree in connection with farm implements than in connection with most other consumer items.
It is our policy to continue to fill those needs. That is why we are fighting the supply situation; and I may say we regard agricultural implements as having the highest priority in the division of available supplies. In the matter of pig iron, material that is in exceedingly short supply, we are robbing other industries in order to see that the agricultural implement industry is kept in full production. Throughout the war years the administrator of the wartime prices and trade board responsible for farm implements was fighting the battle of the implement industry in a very aggressive manner. It is because of his vigilance and because of the vigilance of this government at Washington that we have maintained our imports from that country; and the reason we have been well treated is that we have shared with the United States the burden of taking care of the agricultural implement requirements of the devastated countries. I sincerely hope the speech made by my hon. friend is not broadcast in Washington, because if it is, it may very well follow that the position concerning tractors may be reviewed in the light of comments made in this House of Commons.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of your ruling the motion moved by the hon. gentleman has had to be amended, and it now includes only two matters. It is claimed that the situation in the west with respect to the shortage of farm machinery is serious because of the large crop. There is no doubt about that. It is "in consequence of this that the present situation exists". The members of the C.C.F. and most Liberals have contended all along that the agricultural implement industry was a free trade industry. The protection which was 32 per cent when the present government came into office has been cut down to seven per cent.
Only the war saved the remains of that great industry in Ontario. The Massey-

Farm Implements
Harris company built up a large factory in Toronto under the system of protection. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has referred to this, and it seems to me that he is the only Liberal on the government side who wears the mantle and tie of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He was not a free trader, but a protectionist, and the protection afforded by Sir Wilfrid in 1897 was the same as in 1896. As I say, the hon. gentleman seems to wear the mantle of Elijah-of Sir Wilfrid- and now it would seem the hon. gentleman himself is Elisha because he is the only Liberal on the government side who is ready to defend the principles of the national policy which built up this great agricultural implement industry. Elijah divided the waters of the Jordan, but the hon. gentleman is trying to unite the waters of the Ottawa.	.
Shortly after I came to the house I remember the council of agriculture coming down here in the early twenties with Mr. Drury, then premier of Ontario, and contending that protection was an unmitigated evil, that the manufacturers of farm machinery throughout the country were a lot of robbers and extortionists. They asked that the protection which was afforded should be destroyed. What has been the effect?
The war devastated the agricultural implement industry throughout the world. As I said before, the industry in Toronto engaged in war work and were thus able to keep open. Massey-Harris is established on King street west of Shaw street. This very large industry in conversion is now manufacturing many articles that are necessary and useful. In 1937 and 1938 I contended in this house that the government should give assistance to this industry which was in a serious condition. I also contended that large storage reservoir facilities be built up in England. In 1936, 1937 and 1938 I was the only member in this house who urged that storage reservoirs be established in the old country so that stocks of grain could be built up because I saw that war was surely coming. The British Medical Association said at a meeting in 1938 in London that this grain could be kept in good condition for ten years in such reservoirs.
You have to consider the cause and effect of the two situations set out in this motion. As I said, away back in the twenties the agricultural industry operated under a system of protection. Drastic reductions were made in the budgets of the twenties, and in the thirties the protection was down to seven per cent, as a result many of these industries were forced to the wall.
The grain growing industry was never a free trade industry. It should be the best
protected one for us. It was never a north and south industry but an east and west industry to Britain, France, Italy, and our old allies as well.
What has been the result since Mr. Drury and the council of agriculture came down here in 1923? During the war we saw hon. members to your left, sir, standing up in the house and urging nine, ten, eleven and twelve different forms of protection for the great grain growing industry. Some of them supported the middlemen and elevators and the Winnipeg grain exchanges which were fleecing the dirt farmer out of the profits he should have got from his crops. They were the people to blame for the conditions that then prevailed on the prairies. It. was not the man who sowed the crop, because he was a good man and true. Men of that type were a blessing to the country. You have to look at the cause and effect of the policies then put into force by hon. gentlemen to your left.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) when he came here supported those free trade policies, and there were many others. The result was that the small protection enjoyed by this industry was cut down to seven per cent. Mr. Speaker, you come from western Ontario and you know that in the early days there were manufacturers who wanted to claim all the benefits of protection for themselves. In the twenties those manufacturers were the worst enemies protection had. Protection as properly applied in the days of the Conservative party, and in practice continued by Sir Wilfrid and Mr. Fielding and others, was not applied for the benefit of one class; it was applied for the benefit of the people. The application of protection in that way meant that we were able to maintain our own markets for our own products and for our own workmen. By this national policy of the Conservative government the great cities of this country were built up.
That policy has never been seriously interfered with as it relates to the agricultural implement industry'. The protection was cut down so low that two or three companies were driven to the wall. They could not pay their taxes and overhead charges on the seven per cent. What was the result of the policy of hon. members to your left? The market was left to the American manufacturers. McCormick's in Chicago were able to ship farm implements across the border and avoid taxes.
I have the deepest sympathy for the people of the prairie provinces, especially the grain growers, and all along I have supported their cause in the house. However, I fail to see where this is an emergency, because it has
Farm Implements

been referred to many times during this session. Instead of talking for days about the price of wheat, as is done each session, we might think more about the people of the mother country who were our steady and best customers for grain. I believe we should have given them 200,000 bushels of wheat and saved the mother country from having to put in bread rationing. That would have been a blessing because they were the pioneers and the best friends of the great grain growing industry, as were the people of France and the people of our old ally, Italy. I appreciate the sincerity of the mover of the motion and others to your left, but they are not following the policies they and all their predecessors used to follow when they were free traders. Now that the war is over I am afraid that without adequate protection this industry may have to close up as was demanded in 1923 when the council of agriculture came down here. We shall either have to have adequate protection for the industry or free trade in agricultural implements, and that is what we are heading for. The old Conservative party were absolutely right and always have been. They were the best friends the farmers on the prairies ever had-not the free traders who forget all about cause and effect. We need a policy that will preserve our own markets for our own products and our own work for our own workmen. It is the fallacies of hon. gentlemen to my left which are responsible for the decline in the agricultural implement industry. Some of the manufacturers themselves in the early days were the worst enemies that protection ever had, because they wanted to claim all the benefits of it for themselves and none for the consumer or at times for their workmen or for the country at large. There is a shortage now of agricultural implements, it must be admitted. but there is also a world shortage of suitable farm machinery, and transportation and strikes play an important part in that shortage. There is no doubt that with harvest coming on the situation is serious, but not because of all the reasons put forward by the hon. member for Melfort.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house more than a few moments, but I should like to put some actual figures on the record. I am really surprised at the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) presenting only one side of this picture. I think he should have considered the best interests of the farmers of Saskatchewan and of the rest of Canada before he undertook to speak as he did this morning.

This subject came up in our veterans affairs committee, where the question was raised about the exporting of farm implements. We went to the trouble to get the actual figures We already of course knew quite well that practically all our imports of the most vital farm implement we have-the tractor-are from the United States. We also know that there are people in the United States, just as there are in Canada, who talk in the same manner as the hon. member for Melfort did this morning, that they need their own tractors in the United States and therefore the government of the country should place an embargo on the export of American tractors and let other countries get along as best they can without them. But in the United States the attitude of give-and-take, of carrying on on a comradely basis, prevailed over this argument, and so they continued to export to us our fair share of tractors and other farm implements.
I ask any member representing a farm community in this house what would have happened to the farming industry in Canada if the United States had actually listened to arguments similar to those made this morning by the hon. member for Melfort and discontinued the export of their tractors? Can it be suggested for a single moment that if we took that attitude, if we stopped all shipments of farm machinery to the unfortunate peoples of Europe so that they could raise crops and feed their starving women and children-

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Boo-hoo.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Someone may sneer at that. I do not want to name the member who did it, because I am sure that, on second thought he will be sorry for it. It ill behooves any hon. member to sneer because we are a country most blest by Providence, and if we took the selfish attitude indicated by that "boo" we would not be showing gratitude to divine Providence for the way in which Canada has been blest in a world torn by suffering and starvation. Is it to be suggested that if we did take that attitude towards the unfortunate peoples of Europe and refused to send the farm machinery we are sending to them through UNRRA we could still go to the United States and ask them to ship to us a fair share of their tractors? They would almost certainly say to us: You are not as badly off as the peoples of Europe, and if you are placing an embargo on the shipment of farm machinery to them and also to our farmers, we will hand out to you the same measure of justice that you are handing out to them and to us. The future organization of the world cannot be on the basis of going

Farm Implements
amongst one's own people and saying: "Why are we sending abroad this machinery and this food that we need at home?" and thus working up hatred and antagonism towards international cooperation, which is the only sound basis for world peace and cooperation.
Now I wish to put on Hansard the actual figures tabled in our veterans affairs committee on June 28, to indicate that if we stopped exporting farm machinery and had that same policy applied to us, not only would we lose on the most vital piece of farm machinery we need, the tractor, but we would lose on the total amount of farm machinery available to us. We cannot have it both ways. That was the old idea of the protectionists-that you could stop buying and go on selling abroad. Here are the figures.
In 1939 the gross selling value at the works of our production of farm implements and machinery was $16,000,000 odd. Our imports were $20,000,000; our exports and reexports $7,000,000. That meant an apparent consumption in 1939 of $29,000,000 worth of farm implements in this country, which was $13,000,000 worth more than we produced in 1939.
In 1945 we produced $46,400,000 worth of farm implements. We imported $27,300,000; we exported $20,200,000. Our apparent consumption was $53,500,000 worth, or $7,100,000 worth more of farm machinery consumed than we were able to manufacture in this country.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that in spite of the gloomy outlook of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), in 1945 we actually produced in Canada $46,400,000 worth of farm machinery, as against $16,000,000 worth in 1939. I would also point out that in 1945 while we imported $27,300,000 worth, we exported only $20,200,000 of farm implements, so we gained on the whole transaction approximately $7,000,000 worth of farm machinery, and that farm machinery was the most vital of all to our farmers on the western plains, tractors being a large item of it.
In 1946. from January to April, we imported $16,400,000 worth of farm implements, and exported $10,600,000 worth. In other words, in that period we imported three dollars' worth of farm machinery for every two dollars' worth that we exported.
The proposal of the hon. member would strike at our importations of machinery, including tractors, of which, as I have just said, we imported from January to April three dollars' worth for every two dollars' worth that we exported. It means that we would have $6,000,000 worth less of farm machinery if we did not export and import. I leave it to the
judgment of the house and of the country whether that would be in the best interests of the farmers of Canada.
We hear a great deal in Saskatchewan about these nefarious interests which are exporting in order to make a profit, that they do not care about the farmers' needs, and so on. It is perhaps a good thing that this question has been raised on the floor of the house, because it shows that on balance we have gained during the period from January to April of this year almost $6 million worth of machinery over what we would have had if we had not exported and imported.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Six million dollars is our total apparent consumption in 1932.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yes. For people to go around the country in order to stir up a feeling like this, making demands on their government which might have the most serious repercussions in their effect upon the farmers, and in particular for this to be done by any party or any member in this house, is, I think, very much out of place. However, I am glad that the matter was brought up on the floor of the house, because when it is said around the country many people do not think of the other side at all. They say, "Why are we exporting all this stuff?" They do not think that if we stopped exporting we would stop importing. That is true with regard to the very thing that hon. members have been speaking about-tractors. I venture to say that every one of them came from the United States.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And combine engines.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Perhaps combine engines too. Tractors, anyway. If the ultimate result of the hon. member's speech were what he appeared to wish it to be, these very people would have no tractors at all. It is quite true that a plant to manufacture tractors for cooperatives is being set up in Brantford, but the basis on which that implement industry which is to supply the cooperatives of Canada and the United States is to be built up is this. In times past it was found that owing to the comparatively smaller demand for tractors in Canada compared with the United States, tractors cost more to manufacture in Canada than in the United States. If we did not permit the free importation of tractors the farmer would be paying more for his tractor, because, owing to the smaller output it could not be made in Canada nearly as cheaply as in the United States. As a result of the policy of this government in taking the tariff off it is now possible for the implement industry to supply the cooperatives in the United States and the cooperatives to be set up in Canada,

which will result in a very much larger output because it will supply the cooperatives in the United States. Hon. members on the other side-the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe)-have emphasized the fact that we are getting a large amount of imports in the form of machinery from the United States. Well, first of all, that points to the absurdity of our exporting machinery when we have a chronic deficiency of machinery in this countiy and are having to import it.
The hon. member for Rosthern said that we have a moral obligation to the devastated areas of Europe which are short of machinery. Let me ask the hon. member for Rosthern, or any member of the government, what is the main shortage in Europe to-day? The answer is food. what is the most efficient use which can be made of machinery to-day, and I think it can be proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that more bushels per machine can be produced in Canada than anywhere in Europe.
We in western Canada are suffering a great loss of production on account of the shortage of machinery. To-day in western Canada we are facing, I hope, a very large crop; the present situation looks good, and if that large crop comes we are going to lose millions of bushels of wheat because of the lack of machinery.
There is another thing: this chronic shortage of machinery is having an adverse effect on machinery prices. Old machinery is selling at higher figures than the list prices of new machinery.
In the discussion of loans to foreign countries we in this group pointed out that we were prepared to support these loans purely on one ground, and that was the moral obligation to make them, but that it was not to the advantage of Canada to finance exports of goods which were in short supply in this country; that these loans should be used mainly for the exporting of any goods which happened to be surplus. As I said, Europe is depending on us for tremendous quantities of food; therefore it is essential that our production be kept up at the maximum level, and that can be done only if our farmers have the machinery needed for that maximum production. Therefore I would urge upon the government the desirability of curtailing exports until that chronic deficiency has been made up.

speechtext:
He was referring to the policy of the government and what they had done with regard to exports. The hon. gentleman has had his little say and has presented his case; I wish to make my speech now.
To-day we have one of the largest crops that we have ever seen, east and west. Western Canada went through ten years of depression prior to the war, and all machinery was worn out. The farmers were unable to get new machinery, and they tried to keep what they had in a state of repair. The prices of repair parts have gone up until the farmers are in desperate straits, and now that a bumper crop is expected in some areas where there has not been a crop in years, the farmer does not know how he will manage to take the crop out. This is an emergency situation, and it is the situation that has given rise to this resolution.
We think that machinery should be sent to UNRRA and to other places in order to promote production. It is a matter of meeting the immediate need, and the question is whether you will take tractors and combines and ship them to Greece or Belgium or southern countries where they will not have a harvest for another six months, or whether you will use the equipment in Canada to-day. That is the point. If you ask the people of those countries whom UNRRA is feeding whether they would take a carload of farm machinery, or wheat from western Canada, I have no doubt they would reply at once: Send us the wheat now and the machinery lalter, because we need the food. Reports from UNRRA depict a terrific situation; for they indicate that death from starvation can hardly be averted among the thousands of people who need foodstuffs. In a situation such as this, can we see food in western Canada

Farm Implements
lying in the fields, freezing, rotting, rusting, spoiling in the stooks for lack of machinery?
To me that is the situation. Canada's capacity to produce that food in the next few weeks is the important thing. Take all the machinery we can get hold of to-day and ship it out to that western country. We have another year to carry on our production. It will be of no use to bring in that policy and ship out the machinery in two months' time. It will be too late. That is all we want. We want something done immediately. We are not asking that exports to other countries be stopped. We understand these things have to go on, but we do say that there is an immediate situation which has to be met. We have to meet it now.
People wonder why this shortage continues. They do not understand it. I believe the debate will do something toward enlightening the people as to Canada's productive capacity. Whenever there is a great shortage the pressure for producing is greater and the prices are apt to go up. The wartime prices and trade board does not always keep prices under control. Second-hand tractors were sold this spring in western Canada for $600 or $700 above the price of a new tractor. Why were these prices not controlled? Farmers would pay double the price for a binder to-day if they could get hold of it. We must prevent the building up of a black market; that kind of thing should not be permitted.
What we should like to see done with respect to this particular motion is that the government take immediate cognizance of the fact that there might be a spoilage and a wastage of food which is right there, practically in the bag, at a time when the world is starving. Let the government take hold of the supply of all the machinery that is available in the country and all that it can get from anywhere * else, and put it into that western country to relieve the immediate situation which is facing the people there. This would help to save the food which could be sent abroad to feed a starving world. The whole matter of stepping up the production in the farm implement business to meet these needs-it is too late for this 37ear-should be taken well in hand. The government should make a complete survey of the farm machinery productive capacity of Canada, with a view to imDroving conditions in our own country if the imports cannot be obtained from other countries.

I have no intention of delaying the house at any length on this matter, because it has been fully discussed and probably will bring about some improvement. I am sure that the statement which was made by the
Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and also the statement made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) will clear up the situation considerably. However,
I do wish to clear up one matter, if I can. Close to eleven o'clock last night the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) came over to me and was kind enough to say that he intended to bring up this matter in the house. He did not know just when it would be done. He again read the answers which I gave him some time ago on this subject. At that time I suggested to him that there would be an opportunity to bring up the matter when we were going into supply, and that it could be done satisfactorily then; therefore I was surprised when the question was raised to-day.
This subject is not one in which the Department of Finance alone is interested or should take the sole responsibility. It affects three other departments. The question whether we should or should not export farm machinery is one of government policy.
I think the present policy is a good one, and the only one that Canada can adopt. So far as our trading with the United States is concerned, if we had not been willing to trade in many articles with that country I do not know what would have happened to us. We have been in short supply in steel ever since the beginning of the war. At all times they were ready to share their steel with us, particularly when we were in a much more serious position than we are at the present time. Had we not been willing to adopt that trade policy, the good neighbour policy, the chances are there would have been considerably less farm machinery than we have been getting.
From the point of view of good business I think it should be the policy of Canada to look after our trade abroad. It probably will not be long before these very same people will be crying for more work for our men. If we close the door to-day on machinery for export, or anything else that we can export, they will be the first to complain that work is not available. In my opinion Canada should endeavour to hold on to what export trade she has at present. I shall give the house an illustration. Quite recently an advertisement appeared in our home paper. It was placed there by the Hudson's Bay company. What were they advertising in Victoria? Fancy biscuits manufactured in England. England wanted to continue to hold that market. Some may ask why we are sending food to Britain and they are sending food back to us. There was probably not more than an ounce of food value in those biscuits, but there was a large monetary
Farm Implements

value in them. England was going to hold her trade in the future. I think it was good policy for her to do that. It may not have been good policy for the Hudson's Bay people to put it on the front page of the paper where it would be read by people who do not think and do not understand the ramifications of this kind of business. I-think England was doing the right thing, and we are doing the right thing in this regard.
So far as farm machinery is concerned I think the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) made the situation clear. In only one year since 1931 have Canada's exports been more than her imports. That year was 1933. In every other year we have been debtors so far as farm machinery is concerned. I have not the figures with me, but I want to say something about our own consumption or delivery of goods to the farmers. I have not the figures because when I asked the question over the telephone I was told that they could not give it by provinces; they did say however, that in the first four months the delivery of farm machinery to the farmers of Canada was twenty per cent more than it was in the other years. Up to date we have already delivered to our own people some $10,600,000 worth of farm machinery. Last year our requirements were $53,000,000 in all. Therefore we are well ahead, and if we continue with our production this year the way we did last year we shall produce in the neighbourhood of $60,000,000 worth of farm machinery.
As soon as I got around to the questions this morning I asked the department to prepare a comprehensive statement which I might be able to give to the house on this subject, and I shall do so on a later occasion. That is all I wish to say at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to hold up the business of the house, but I do want to make a few references to the trend this debate has taken. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) I think has rendered a public service in introducing this resolution, which is to the effect that there is an emergency in the west in the matter of the supplies of farm implements required for the harvesting of this year's crop.
Much has been said on the question of foreign trade. Personally I cannot see where that question enters into this discussion at all. We have in western Canada to-day an emergent situation which demands action now, not consideration by the government of questions of trade. In the few moments at my disposal I have taken the trouble to get some statistics

which indicate that the government has been negligent in discharging its responsibility in the matter of providing for reapers, reaper-threshers, combines and the like, necessary for the harvesting of our crop. This is not a new problem. The government was aware last April of the condition and of the necessity of increasing the supply of farm machinery this year, because that was the reason given for the increase in price. The 12% per cent increase was to assure the production of farm implements in order to meet the increasing demand of this country. One of the major considerations then before the Department of Agriculture, and I believe the Department of Trade and Commerce as well, was the necessity of making available the necessary farm machinery to replace that which had become obsolete during the war but which had continued to be used because no replacements were available.
What has the government done? It realized that under normal conditions a large crop was to be harvested this year. It has known that for a period of months, but it strikes me as very strange that in June alone, at a time when the government must have fully realized the situation, exports of harvesters, binders, reaper-threshers and the like from this country were materially greater than they were a year ago. In the period from January to November,
1945,	Canada exported 9,729 harvesters and binders. In the six months ended June 30,
1946,	our exports totalled 8,083, or almost as many in six months as had been exported in eleven months in 1945. Take reaper-threshers; to-day in the western provinces particularly agriculture is mechanized. Without combines, labour being in short supply as it is to-day, our crops will not be marketed. What is the record'? From January to November, 1945, the number of combines exported from this country was 1,888. For the six months ended June 30, 1946, the exports totalled 2,616. I could go through the list of threshing machine separators and so on, showing material increases at a time when the government must have realized-and it is not so much averse to exercising certain types of controls-what the condition was going to be. Take the month of June as an example. During that month, with the great crop coming along in western Canada, which must have been known to the government, Canada exported 473 combines, 1,599 reapers and 1,073 mowing machines, harvesters and binders. One can sometimes excuse the necessity for trade, but at the moment the greater necessity is the harvesting and preservation of that food in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I would not be holding up this matter any longer except that only one hon. member from Manitoba has spoken. I think it should be understood that this question affects Manitoba as much as any other province in Canada.
I was a little surprised at the attitude taken by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in his reply to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). Instead of showing some appreciation for the fact that the hon. member for Melfort had taken the trouble to bring this serious matter to the attention of the government, the hon. member for Rosthern attempted to scold him. I do not think that is what this house expected. I realize that the government cannot be conversant with everything that develops throughout the country, and there are many things which possibly slip by unnoticed. It may be that they were not aware of the serious shortage of farm implements on the prairies, and the hon. member for Melfort has performed a public service for all the farmers of Canada by bringing this matter up for discussion to-day.
I think he made it abundantly clear that the only reason he was bringing it up at this time was its urgent importance. In some parts of the prairies harvesting has already begun, while in most other parts harvesting will begin in the next few weeks. There is a definite shortage of implements, and I think the government should have taken a more cooperative attitude than it appeared to take to-day.
A great deal has been said about the export of implements and the possible effects of preventing exports to other countries. So far as I am concerned I would be the last to say that we should place an embargo against the
Farm Implements

export of any materials to countries which require them, provided that we can spare them. To the extent that we can spare farm implements or anything else, we should be prepared to export them to countries which need them. But we are faced with an immediate shortage of implements in this country just before the harvest season begins.
It should be understood that if we export reapers and harvesters to the United States or to European countries they will not arrive there in time for use in harvesting. For the most part harvesting in the United States is either completed or well advanced, and the same may be said of many European countries. Anything we might ship now would not reach those countries in time to help with their harvesting. This should be clearly understood. It is not a question of depriving other countries of harvesting equipment which they might be able to use; it is a matter of making available to the farmers of western Canada, and all Canada, implements which have been manufactured and which are lying in pools, perhaps consigned to other countries but not yet shipped. I do not think it is unreasonable for members of this group or anyone else to request the government to give immediate consideration to releasing some of these implements which if shipped to other countries will not turn a wheel for a whole year while we are suffering a shortage in this country.

I do not know, but if one bushel of wheat is likely to be wasted because of a shortage of implements which are lying around and not being used, we should try to see that it is not wasted.
I think the argument about exports and imports was beside the point. I would not mind if we were to have a full dress discussion on imports and exports, because I am sure hon. members on all sides could contribute something to it. But I would point out that there seems to be a metamorphosis occurring in the thinking of hon. members on the Liberal side and hon. friends to my right in the matter of exports and imports. It was not so long ago that hon. members who support the government used to tell this house and the country that we must export in order to have a favourable balance of trade. That was their story then, but to-day they say we must export in order that we may have imports in exchange. I congratulate them upon that changed attitude; I believe it is far more sound, f think it was the present leader of the

opposition (Mr. Bracken) who not very long ago coined the phrase that we must export or die. I may be wrong in crediting that phrase to him, but I think that is where it came from.

subtopic: SHORTAGE IN WESTERN CANADA-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Hon. members on all sides are beginning to realize that we export in order that we may get goods in exchange, not to bring about a mythical balance of trade, which was the argument advanced before. Bringing in the argument of exports and imports at this time seemed to me to be getting a little away from the subject. I believe all the hon. member for Melfort wanted to do, and he presented his case ably, was to rivet the attention of the government on the shortage of implements in the west and throughout Canada generally, so that in the next twenty-four hours they might do something to supply implements which are already available but are being held or consigned to other countries. I do not think that is unreasonable.
The argument that people in the United States might feel offended if we refused to give them implements which normally might go there is not a very good one. I have been in the United States several times and I have spoken with farmers and others. I found these people most reasonable. I do not think they would object to the Canadian people supplying their own farmers with implements when there is a great need for them rather than ship them across the border. I believe they understand our situation, and I submit we are underestimating the friendliness and understanding of the people of the United States when we say that they would feel offended or would take some action in reprisal. I do not think that is correct.
It is not because of politics that we bring this matter to the attention of the house. I have in my hand a letter addressed to the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) by the Saskatchewan associated boards of trade. Most of the members of this association are not farmers, but they recognize the shortage of certain types of implements. They say:

Farm Implements
There is much concern in Saskatchewan and I presume on the prairies generally, that there will not be sufficient vehicles to transport the current crop from the farms to the rail head, in order to expedite its delivery to the peoples who are so much in need of it.
A little further down they make the following recommendation:
The Saskatchewan associated boards of trade respectfully urge that of the available supply, increases lie made in the ordinary current allotment of commercial vehicles, or that quotas for winter months be diverted to fall delivery in time for the crop season.
It is evident that the associated boards of trade of Saskatchewan are aware of the impending shortage for this harvest. In all fairness the government should not take this merely as something in respect to which we are criticizing them, but as something that we have brought to their attention because we feel it is necessary that they take immediate action. I hope that is the spirit in which they will take it eventually.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words in support of the motion of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). I do not want it to be thought that the western part of Canada is the only part of this country that is short of implements. Instead of the Shortage being merely a western problem, it is a national catastrophe. It has been brought about by the shortsighted policy of the government in granting export licences for such a large percentage of our farm implements. True, we want an export market, but surely we do not want it at the disadvantage of our own Canadian producers, especially in view' of the great scarcity of farm labour this year. Even though some people may not realize it, crops that are ready to harvest will not wait. If I may be pardoned a personal reference, I have had a 15-run fertilizer hoe drill on order for three years, and up to this spring it was not available. I had to get a disc drill to take its place; otherwise I would have had no drill at all.
r.Mr. J. A. Ross.]
Here is another special case. A man had a tractor ordered for two years, and he had already bought some of the implements to go with that tractor. Being assured that the tractor would be available in 1946, he sold his last team of horses last fall. He has not received the tractor, and only for his good fortune in being able to borrow one from a neighbour was he able to save half a canning factory pea crop. I can cite dozens of other cases in my own community where people have been working at a great disadvantage on account of the shortage of agricultural implements.
We are told that the shortage is caused by strikes, shortages of materials and so an, but we find on investigation, that a little more than $14,000,000 worth of implements were exported from this country in the first six months of 1946. The present situation is not the result of shortages. It is the result of the shortsighted policy of this government in allowing that volume of implements to be exported when we are in terrible need of them right here at home. W'hy is this so? The reason is obvious when, you compare the prices of these implements in Canada with the prices procured for them in various foreign countries. I say to the government that even at this late date it may still save part of the crop in western Canada and eastern Canada by allowing some of these implements destined for export to be retained to meet the domestic demand.
Mr. F. W. TOWNLEY-SMITH (North Battleford): Mr. Speaker, the motion calls attention to the urgency of the need of farm machinery in order to take off this year's crop. The discussion has wandered all over the well-known half acre. The amazing thing to me is that there should be any argument or debate about this at all. It is a condition which could have been and should have been anticipated and taken care of by the government, but this was not done.
To come right back to the actual matter. Does anyone argue about the importance of food? I do not think so. Does anyone argue that the western crop is not heavy? I do not think so. Does anyone argue that it is not within a few days of being harvested? Again I do not think so. Does anyone argue that in the west machines are not badly worn and badly in need of replacement? No argument has been made about these matters. That is really the subject matter of the motion-the need of more machinery, of new machinery. Instead of that, we get into an abstract discussion or debate on our export trade, and even at that we discuss principally exports into the United States. The statement has been made to-day that some seventy-one countries

Questions
were receiving Canadian machinery, that exports were being made to all those countries. Well, what about the other sixty-nine, if we are just discussing exports into the United States and to those countries which have been devastated by war? The need for these machines is undoubtedly very great. The fact that the crop is heavy simply aggravates the situation, because a machine which is capable of taking care of a farm crop of ordinary, normal proportions is not able to cut a crop which is extraordinarily heavy; and I fear that as soon as harvesting operations begin there will be great distress among the farmers who are attempting to use worn-out machines.
My suggestion is that, since the situation in the United States is practically cared for now-at the end of July and beginning of August all arrangements for their harvest have been made, they have the machines, and if they have not got them they have managed in some way without them-the urgency which you, Mr. Speaker, are allowing us to discuss is in our own country, and for the time being, anyway, the great concentration should be on our own particular problem, for which purpose we should stop exports for the present and see to it that the west is supplied with the machines which, I believe, are necessary in order to take off this most important crop.
