Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved the second reading of bill No. 329, to amend the Pension Act.
He said: Since I dealt with this matter yesterday I have just two words to say. In the first place I believe the committee on veterans affairs practically unanimous in regard to at least the general principles of this legislation. In the second place the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the parliamentary assistant, will have the honour to direct and pilot the legislation through the house.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Yesterday the minister made a concise statement with reference to the matters which had been before the veterans committee. As he indicated, these matters have been carefully considered for many weeks. We dlid come to an agreement as to the procedure to be followed with reference to these bills. We agreed that any discussion which took place would be not on the resolutions but on second reading.
As the minister pointed out, this has been a long and tedious task for the members of the committee. We met sometimes itwo and three times a day. Speaking for myself-and I know that my experience was that of every other hon. member of the committee-I found it difficult at times to carry on other duties so far as the House of Commons was concerned.
The minister will agree that we were not unanimous on all bills. Neither was the committee unanimous on all the recommendations with respect to individual bills. I think I can say with regard to some of the bills that possibly there was unanimous consent. Others were carried by the majority vote of the committee. While still others had the
majority support of the committee, they were changed to suit the will and pleasure of the government. That is a fair statement to make.
I agree with the minister that a prolonged discussion of these bills is unnecessary. These matters have 'been discussed in the committee for some weeks. All the arguments pro and con have been advanced; and they can be found in the reports of the committee. However, there are certain things which hon. members would like to mention in the house. I *was much interested yesterday afternoon in the minister's remarks. Since I was a member of the committee I was pleased with the eulogy he paid to the work of the committee. I am also looking forward to the presentation of the medals to which the minister says the members are deserving. I should also like to point out that while the minister rather takes all the credit for the veterans' charter-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Not to himself, no. While he gives credit for it to the committee, and possibly to his own actions as minister over the last number of years, I think in all modesty that we cannot take all the credit. This veterans' charter is not the product, of the present committee; it is the prodiuct of many years of work of committees which have met' in the past. Take our Pension Act as an example. It is not the product of the work of the 1946 committee. As a matter of fact we made few changes in it. The Pension Act has been an evolution from 1916, when the first committee was set up, down to the present time. Hundreds of members of different parliaments who sat on previous committees also deserve credit for this so-called veterans' charter. Credit is also due to organizations entirely outside of parliament. I wish to pay tribute to the men of the Canadian Legion. I 'believe there would be no veterans' charter to-day if it were left entirely to the members of the House of Commons. The results of our work have been based partly on the recommendations made by the Canadian Legion, the Canadian Corps Association, and the Amputations Association. I could mention the Canadian army and navy veterans association and many others which have contributed to a great extent to this so-called veterans' charter of which the minister spoke yesterday.
As to its being the finest committee that has sat, I will agree with that, but in reading over the names of some of the men, who have headed committees in the past I must say that I have been greatly impressed by their stature both in public and in private life. There was Mr. W. F. Nickle, an outstanding man in his
Pension Act

time. There was Mr. Newton. W. Rowell, an outstanding man of his time, Mr. Hume Cronyn, Sir Herbert Marler, the Hon. Cyrus Macmillan, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), also a member of this committee. May I also add, Mr. Speaker, that he is an hon. member who had the affection of the soldiers of the last war and has at least the affection of the men of the air force of this war. Therefore we cannot claim all the credit when we consider the names of the men who have worked hardl on committees in the past.
The minister paid a tribute to our chairman. We all enjoyed working under the chairman. We did not always agree with him. Sometimes we were afraid that he might blow up, but fortunately it did not happen. I will agree that he is deserving of a medal. I would also suggest that not only is he deserving of a medal in the work he did in the veterans' committee, but he should get a bar to his medal for going out to lead the Liberal party in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: He ought to get the V.C. for that.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: That is a great act of bravery,.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
It is not my intention to review, as the minister did yesterday, all the legislation which is to come before us. We have the Pension Act before us at the present time. The introduction of the Pension Act creates great interest not only here but also throughout the country, because it is the expression, through its representatives, of Canada's intention to provide for those who have suffered most in the defence of this country and of civilization. In their gratitude the Canadian people should feel, and I am sure do feel, that the best is none too good. We sometimes compare our veterans' legislation and our Pension Act with the legislation of other countries, and perhaps make comparisons without knowing the facts. I am not going to belittle Canadian legislation relating to veterans; I think possibly it is as good as the legislation anywhere in the world. Not long ago I read an article in a United States magazine in which it was claimed that they had the best legislation, so perhaps it is a case of each man thinking his own home is the best. However, I am satisfied that our legislation is good. It should be. There is no reason why Canada should not make provision as good as if not better than that of any other country in the world, because I believe Canada came through the war better than any other country. That is so for many reasons. In the first place,

of course, we were a long distance from the scene of conflict and had no cities or towns destroyed. Our countryside was not devastated. Apart from the great loss we suffered in young manhood, Canada was not greatly disturbed or greatly troubled. So perhaps when we compare our legislation with that of Great Britain, whose cities were devastated from one end of the country to the other; with that of France or Holland or Belgium, or the enemy countries of Italy and Germany, we are not actually comparing comparable things. So I say there is no reason at all why we should not have the finest veterans legislation anywhere in the world.	-
This legislation, I believe, can be divided into two distinct classes. First, and very important, is the legislation providing for the men who returned to this country sound in body and in mind. These are the young men who went over to fight our battles and who returned to take their place in civilian life. We have passed a good deal of legislation affecting these young men; but I sometimes wonder what is their reaction when, after fighting overseas for five years or more, a year after the end of the war they find the present chaotic condition in regard to labour and industry. I am not going to blame either industry or labour for this situation, since a committee of this house is considering the matter at the present time, but it must be the subject of serious thought on the part of these young men who gave years of their lives in the defence of liberty to find a certain amount of chaos in the country, with more in prospect. There are two things in particular which these young men want. They lost four or five years of their lives as far as education is concerned, and it is the duty of the government, the duty of the people of Canada, to see that they are provided with educational opportunities. This is being done in a large way by the government and the country; but the principal thing a young man wants, coming back to Canada to-day, is the opportunity to earn a living. We sometimes hear irresponsible people, both ex-soldiers and civilians, say, "Oh, the country owes me a living." The country does not owe any man a living. The country does owe every young man and woman in this country an opportunity to make a living. It also owes them an opportunity to establish homes for themselves, where they can bring up their children with proper educational facilities and in pleasant surroundings. These are the two things which I believe should be kept in mind in regard to the reestablishment of our young men who have returned from the war.

Pension Act
The second and probably most important class of legislation deals with the men who have come back maimed in body and mind, and the dependents of those who lost their lives overseas. They are supposed to be protected by the Pension Act and its amendment. It would take me a long time to go into the different sections of this act and comment upon them; as a matter of fact we received it only a few minutes ago. Yesterday the minister emphasized that one great principle was to be included in the act; that is, the insurance principle. We remember that this principle formed part of the Pension Act for a great many years. It was first enacted in 1919, and was removed in 1940. So while this insurance principle is perhaps the most important feature of this legislation and the most important thing to be done in connection with pension legislation by the committee, we are simply restoring something which was in the act from 1919 to 1940.
There are two principles in connection with Canadian pensions, and I should like to quote something that was said in connection with the 1919 legislation:
The so-called insurance principle. On this basis ex-members of the forces were pensioned not only for any disability "attributable to military service," but as well for any disability "incurred on" service.
That is the explanation of the insurance principle.
Canada insured her soldiers for all disabilities incurred by them during their service period . . .
Commenting on that principle Mr. Rowell said:
Our law as it stands is broader than the pension law in any other country, so far as we know. The insurance feature which I have mentioned is not in any other law, so far as I am aware. 'In that respect we give the soldier the benefit of insurance during the whole period of the war.
That was the attitude in 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: That was Mr. Lemieux and Mr. Rowell, in the 1919 committee.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
And I may say that early in the proceedings of the committee dealing with the Pension Act I moved that the insurance principle be restored. That motion was generally supported by hon. members, and though we were left in doubt by the government for a considerable time, eventually the principle found its way back into the act, and I am sure everyone is very pleased as a result.
Another point gave us considerable concern in the committee, where it was debated on numerous occasions by the hon. member
for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and others, having to do with section 11 (1) (c) of the act, reading as follows:
No deduction shall be made from the degree of actual disability of any member of the forces, who has served in a theatre of actual war during the great war or during the war with the German Reich, on account of any disability or disabling condition which existed in him prior to his period of service in either of the aforesaid wars.
Then it goes on to mention three exceptions:
... no pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which, at the time he became a member of the forces, was wilfully concealed, was obvious or was recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment.
There was no exception taken, but the committee felt, and I think they were expressing the opinion of most returned men, that the phrase "wilfully concealed" should be struck out of the act, and it was so moved by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I believe the committee carried that motion but the department did not feel that this could be done. However, there was a compromise and I see that in the bill, instead of the phrase "wilfully concealed", we have the phrase "wilfully and deliberately concealed." I understood from the members of the commission when this matter was being discussed before the committee that they did not like the words "wilfully concealed." However, apparently they have adopted some modus operandi, if I may call it that, and while a certain stigma against a returned soldier intimating he was concealing something might be implied, I think they got around it in some way in actually carrying out the intentions of the act. I am sorry it is not being taken out now, and I hope at some time in the future it shall be taken from the act.
Another point brought up was in connection with the dateline. I was pleased to hear the minister say yesterday that as far as children of veterans are concerned there will be no dateline with regard to the granting of pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: We can thank the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) for that.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is a fact, that is, provided that the parents are married before May 1, 1944. The minister will remember that this point was the cause of considerable controversy, because it was felt to be unfair that children born after that date should not be given the same opportunity as children bom before. It is a matter of some disappointment that the dateline was not eliminated entirely from the act, that is, as it applies to widows as well as to children. There are
Pension Act

many veterans of the first war who are getting to be comparatively old men and who have lost their first wives. In their later days many of them feel that they would like to have companionship and they marry again. If a veteran marries a second time I do not see why his second wife should not receive the same consideration as a first wife.
We were met with the argument that there might be deathbed marriages, but in looking through the act I find that there is ample protection in that regard. Subsection 2 of section 32 provides that if the death of a husband has occurred less than one year subsequent to the date of marriage and the commission has information that at the time of such marriage he had a reasonable expectation of survival, for at least one year afterward, the matter shall be considered. That section provides for the non-payment of a pension where there is a deathbed marriage.
Another matter discussed extensively in the committee was the question of preenlistment condition. I do not intend to take up the time of the house this afternoon in discussing this matter, because there are other hon. members who will follow me and I am sure they will discuss it fully. There was also the question of the automatic increase in disability pension. Many members of the committee felt that not only should the man who suffered a gunshot wound and who was in receipt of a fifty per cent pension receive a higher entitlement on reaching the respective ages of 55 years, 57 years and 59 years, but that any man who had a disability, whether a gunshot wound or other impairment of health, should have his pension increased. This was not granted.
I should like to say a few words with reference to hospitalization. When overseas in 1942 and again for a short time in 1944 and 1945 I had the opportunity of visiting many of our military hospitals. I do not think I can pay too high a tribute to the work that was done in those hospitals. I think the lower casualties in the last war can be attributed more to the improved science of medicine and the treatment of wounds and disease than to anything else. In those hospitals we had the finest doctors and nurses that it was possible to get. I hope an effort will be made to get the same type of nurse and the same type of doctor for our veterans' hospitals as were in charge of our military hospitals.
There seems to be some overcrowding in the veterans' hospitals at the present time. The minister has increased greatly the number of beds in the different hospitals during the last few years, but there is still some overcrowding. I think it was shortsighted on the

part of the government not to have certain hospitals ready immediately the war was over. We knew there would be a great need for hospitalization. For instance, the hospital in Toronto should have been completed before the war ended.
Large sums of money were expended upon building and equipping military hospitals throughout the country. For instance, three or four hundred thousand dollars were spent upon the military hospital located at Windsor, Nova Scotia. This hospital was located on diked land, and at times the dikes broke and water surrounded the area. The department was advised to build the hospital upon higher ground, but they did not do so. This was one of the best equipped military hospitals in the country. Doctors going overseas who inspected the hospital commented upon the splendid equipment. My submission is that hospitals such as the one at Windsor and those in other parts of Canada should have been built in locations where they could have been used as veterans' hospitals.

There is another matter which was not taken up in the veterans committee but which I think will have to receive the attention not only of parliament but of the country within the next few years. I refer to the plight of our older veterans. I believe there are some seven veterans' homes in Canada, but they are more or less for veterans who need hospitalization. I am referring to the older veteran, the man who perhaps is living alone in some isolated part of the country. There must be hundreds of them. I think we should do what other countries such as Great Britain and the United States have done, build homes in which our older veterans can live. Canada has been engaged in two major wars in the last thirty years, the first great war and the last great war.

Pension Act
It has perhaps not been necessary to have old soldiers' homes in this country hitherto, but I believe the time has now come when we should have homes where these older men can get together and be happy and discuss the battles of the past, or as Goldsmith said, shoulder their crutch and show how wars were won.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer; it has to do with my own section of the dominion. I want to read a statement made by Major General Burns as reported in the Montreal Gazette of July 4 of this year. Speaking of the rehabilitation programme he said:
The department was satisfied with the rate of employment in its various districts across the dominion except for the maritimes, where veterans applying for out-of-work allowance were three times the proportion of elsewhere.
The difficulty there appears to be, the general noted, that in certain regions conditions for employment will not improve particularly and, although some authorities had recommended a programme of public works for the area, the Department of Reconstruction has decided against such measure at the present time. The question that remained was whether migration to other areas should be encouraged.
By the same token, veteran's preference has been effective right across the country except in the maritimes.
It will be noted that General Burns emphasizes four points in that statement. The first is that three times the number of veterans applied for out-of-work benefits in the maritime provinces than applied in other parts of Canada. That indicates one thing, that the opportunities for employment in the martime provinces are not nearly as great as they are in other parte of Canada. It means that we have three times as many veterans out of work in the martimes as there are in any other part of this country.
The second point was that while the authorities had recommended a programme of public works the Department of Reconstruction had decided against it. I have been surprised, Mr. Speaker, that with the amount of unemployment which there has been in Canada, and which there is to-day particularly in the maritimes, some programme of public works has not been started by this government and by the local governments in order to give these young men work.
His third statement was whether migration to other areas should be encouraged. That is a suggestion to which I am sure we in the maritime provinces take strong exception. For too long have our young men from the maritime provinces been migrating elsewhere. Of the class that graduated in engineering from the university of New Brunswick a few months ago, and it was one of the largest 63260-261
engineering classes they had ever had, only two young men could find employment in their native province. We of the maritime provinces want employment for our young people. We want them to have an opportunity to live and work and remain in their own province and not be forced to go to the United States, as tens of thousands of them have had to do in years past, or to the central provinces or to the west. We want them to stay in the maritime provinces. I do urge, upon the government so far as that section of this country is concerned that some public works be started, and be started at once in order to retain the young men from the maritime provinces in their native land and in their own home. I could suggest many public works that could advantageously be started, but I will not take the time of the house to do it to-day.
The fourth point made by General Bums was that the veteran's preference has been effective right across the country except in the maritimes. That simply means that there is more attention paid to political appointments in the maritime provinces than to appointments based on the veteran's preference. I have had many communications with reference to different departments of the government where the veteran's preference is not being observed as it should be. I appeal to the government that in making appointments in all departments of the government the veteran's preference be given every consideration. Only a few days ago I had a letter from a lawyer in the maritime provinces, a man who had a very fine record overseas. He lives in quite a large town, but he gets no work in connection with the Veterans Land Act administration. He writes me that men who never saw service at all are doing all the legal work. This should not be. The returned soldier would rather deal with another returned soldier than with a civilian. I hope that the different departments will check up on this matter.
In closing I should like to pay a tribute to some of the heads of the different branches administering veterans' affairs. I believe that at the head of these branches and departments we have some of the best men it would be possible for us to obtain. I might mention Mr. Woods, the deputy minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs; General Burns, whose statement I have just quoted with respect to the maritimes-and let me say that I was not criticizing him when I quoted his statement because I think the department was fortunate indeed in getting such a man. I will also mention Brigadier Melville, Colonel Garneau and Mr. Murchison. I believe that they all have the interests of the veterans at heart. The difficulty is not

Pension Act

with the men at the head, but rather with the men spread across the country. Sometimes there is too much red tape and too much confusion.
I have nothing to add, Mr. Speaker, except to repeat that I hope that the veteran's preference will be very carefully considered in all appointments made in all the provinces.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Tem-iscouata): Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. and gallant, member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) upon his very fine speech. He has a fine military record, and he loves the soldiers. He himself has done a lot for them. I remember that on the civil service committee several years ago during two sessions he made some most valuable suggestions. I can say the same of my hon. friend the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) who sits in front of him.
I shall not take very long, Mr. Speaker, to express what I have to say on this bill. But first I should like to pay a special tribute to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). He is gifted with a very kind heart, and when there is some difficulty we may appeal to him in confidence of having the wrong redressed. I understand1 that his task is not always easy, but it is made less difficult by the excellent cooperation which he receives from his parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker). Both are good giants, giants in mind as well as in body; they work a lot; they know how to work-which is happening quite seldom in this vicinity-and they do their best to help others. But before going farther, I hope that the minister will be in a position to make an estimate of the approximate cost of these eleven bills. It will be quite heavy, and it is the kind of information which we should have.

speechtext:
Well, I wonder. If my hon. friends like the taxes that the Canadian people will have to pay we could double it, iust because of their liking taxation.
But there are unpopular measures which are necessary, and one, which was suggested years ago by the hon. member for Temis-couata, would be a check-up of all pensions of the first war. At the present time we expend a considerable amount of money for pensions which are paid on account of service in the first world war. Would1 it not be profitable for the country to have an independent check-up made of each case to see if the money goes to those who are entitled to it, or if the circumstances have changed? This would be unpopular, but I remind the minister that a large amount of money can be provided for military' pensions without the expected political return being received. No one forgets that in 1930 the government was lavish with pensions and the government was defeated1, and that in 1935 another government was also lavish and that government was defeated-which means that no one should have a political motive in dealing with matters of the kind.
Another thing which struck me in reading this bill No. 329, to amend the Pension Act is the reference to world war I and world war II which is often repeated in the various sections of the bill. I hope that, in the future, amendments to the Pension Act for world war III will not appear; that we shall stop at world war II. When I think of the pensions to those who are still alive after having been disabled, and when I think of the pensions to the dependents, I have to think also of the fine youth who had to pay the price of war with their own blood, and the loss of powerful brains, young brains, brains of men who could have served their country very well and who lie under white crosses in the cemeteries of Europe and other parts of the world. It impresses me deeply, and I

Pension Act
consider that the country has a duty to perform with regard to those who have been in the army. It is the duty of the collectivity.
But. it is not because a man has been in the army that he is entitled to a pension. He is entitled to it because of certain considerations due to the difficulties he has encountered in service. If a young man has enlisted or has joined the colours and has done his duty either in this country or outside it, has followed the orders of his commanding officer and has done well, and comes back in good health, he is not entitled to any pension. The pension is for the disabled and for the dependents of the departed and of those who are unable to earn their livelihood. It may be that service in the army is a very good and profitable experience to the young man who comes back in good health. But so many are handicapped; so many have suffered wounds, have lost an arm, a leg. an eye or are totally deprived of sight, or have sustained other disabilities that it is impossible to think of them with "a dry heart." I was in close touch with soldiers and veterans during the whole war; I considered it my duty to listen to them and to try to help them out whenever the occasion occurred if it was possible to do so. It was done in various ways, and I saw the close connection that existed between the Department of National Defence and the then Department of Pensions and National Health. It is my duty to pay a special tribute to my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Macdonald), who did so much for the boys when he was parliamentary assistant to the then minister of national defence. His kindness, his thoughtfulness and his conscientious study of long and tedious files brought cheer to many homes. It was not interesting; it was not pleasurable, but in spite of his other occupations he considered it a duty to come to the assistance of young men who were not treated by the medical corps with the consideration that they deserved.
A member of parliament has many things to do, but one of his duties is to listen to those who are in trouble and in difficulty and to try to do something for them, and what I happened to do was to receive in my office some boys who were unfit. In spite of the fact that they were unfit and sometimes disabled, they were graded A by the army. Some were suffering from goitre; others from chronic appendicitis; others had one eye; others had lumps the size of my fist on the spine. They could neither stand nor sit upright. Others suffered from other disabilities. They were, however, all graded A. I have a letter from the department to the effect that they were 63260-2612
fit and that if they complained it was because there was something wrong with their minds rather than with their bodies.
I asked my friend Colonel Desrosiers, who as deputy minister of national defence did so much for the boys, to look into the matter, and these men were submitted to another examination. I asked that they be examined by competent doctors. After instructions from the deputy minister and my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax, they were examined and found unfit; and they were found unfit because of disabilities that existed at the time they were declared fit.
What happened afterwards? They were not given a pension but were told that their unfitness predated their entry into the army, and the matter was left at that. It is cruel; but at least, with the assistance of my hon. friend and the assistance of Colonel Desrosiers, I succeeded in getting them out of the army, because it is my deep conviction, in spite of what has been said about the Pulhems system, that it is absurd to keep in the army, and at the expense of the country, one who is practically unfit. But that is not all. There were times when pensions were granted to everybody, and the expenditure was so great that the tap was turned off so that afterwards no one, not even those who were most meritorious, could get anything. They could not get anything because of the enormous expenditures that had been made carelessly before. It is hard to correct it.
I have some files here. There is, for instance, the file of a man who was in the first world war, No. 897, who was one of the first to join the colours and one of the last to be discharged. He was wounded through the body; but, since he was a big man, his disability was not so apparent at the start and he was discharged A-l. Subsequently, however, he had a premature predisposition to certain disabilities, especially rheumatism. He would probably never have had rheumatism if he had not been five years in the trenches, but because he was classified as A when discharged it was impossible to get anything for him. The facts are there, and his number is 897.
This is not the first time that I have mentioned his case in the house, but I have never succeeded in getting anything because of the stubborness of the officials in the Department of Pensions and National Health. I put the name of Brigadier Melville in brackets because he seems to be well disposed, but there are still many who belong to the old school tie and whom it is impossible to move. I wonder what power is needed to make them move and move sensibly. They are there to effect
Pension Act

economy for the country; but watch their own expenditures for themselves and see how lavish they are, while they are stingy to those who deserve something.
I have another case, No. 23923, a man who had a sore leg when he enlisted 'but who was classified A notwithstanding. He was put in charge of the barracks on 'the hill in Levis in the winter-barracks not needed. They were outside, and there was no place where the men could go and warm themselves in the winter. They were exposed to the wind. This man got a disability but it did not count. His disability was said to have predated his enlistment and therefore he got nothing.
I find it a crime; I find it shameful; and 1 call the attention of the minister and of his assistant to these cases. But I do not speak to deaf ears, because in many cases they have helped me out in spite of the procrastination of some men in the department. In fact, procrastination is a euphemism.
Then there is the case of E-36159,, who suffered a rupture. The rupture was cured and to that extent he is all right, but he suffers from a nervous affection and the explanation given is hot clear.
There is another case right- here in the House of Commons. I mentioned it earlier in the session. It is the case of a man who had a bullet through the cheeks and who was given a fifteen per cent disability. He suffers from cancer. This is an elevator man, No. 889897. I am told that he gets all he should get. Well, if we are ready to open the doors of Canada, and to open the taps of the Pension Act to anyone who comes -here and who belongs -to an allied army and who may be domiciled in Canada within two years after the war, we should do something for our own people first.
There are several cases. The minister and his parliamentary assistant have settled admirably the case of Captain Bellew, V.C., who passed over the head of everybody, including the Canadian Legion, and sent an S.O.S. to the member for Temiseouata, who looked after him with all his heart. I thank the minister and his assistant for what they did in this case. But what they did in the case of Bellew should be done for the elevator man here. We hear a lot about public welfare. There is not one of us who would tolerate a thing like that in his own home, and it is done in the home of all of us. I also believe that those who perform a duty in the House of Commons are entitled to the special consideration of members of parliament, just as old employees who live in a home sometimes for two generations, old servants knowing everybody in the family, give good service

and deserve special consideration. I cannot see a man suffering without trying to help him, and I am sure that is the feeling of all hon. members who are doing me the honour of listening to me at this time.
Speaking of cases, there is something else I would mention. I have murder cases, cases of men of the army who were nearly murdered by the incompetency of the medical corps under Chisholm, that most nefarious man. He was in charge of the medical corps under the Department of National Defence, a most incompetent man, a cruel man. He was responsible for all the suffering of many soldiers who could not get justice, who could not get fair treatment. He is now in charge of the health of the world. What a shame! I do not discuss the theories which he has expounded over the air or in public meetings. I say that man is a criminal because so many men in the army have suffered on account of him, and I have to fight twice as hard because of his stupidity and ignorance.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Poor Santa Claus suffered, too.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I am not talking of Santa Claus; I am talking of the soldiers who have suffered because of the stupidity and incompetence of Chisholm.
I have many murder cases. The Hornblow family of Toronto has sent me a whole file which was transcribed by the hand of the mother of the boy who was killed because of the stupidity of the doctors who did not give him the proper treatment, and the doctors were exonerated. We cannot have justice, because it is precisely the guilty party who supplies the evidence against those who have grounds for complaint. Here is my murder case. He was a fine boy, and his mother is a widow. His number was E-630952. Here was a boy suffering from a heart condition. He did his duty. He was called and reported. He had leave during Christmas about two years ago. He went home and fainted while he was there. He had a certificate from his family doctor that he was suffering from a heart condition. He brought the certificate to the camp and gave it to the sergeant. He was examined. And mark you, sir, I know whereof I speak. He was examined by a heart specialist who found that there was something wrong with him and marked it on the sheet. Then the chairman of the board struck it out and the boy was told to go back to the barracks. He could not do any drill. He asked for a doctor. The doctor was refused. They told him that he was a faker. He asked for a padre. They did not inform

Pension Act
the padre. This faker, according to the words of the sergeant, went to bed. He was found dead fifteen or twenty minutes afterwards. Those who were there reported that his face was crimson when he went to bed, because he was suffering from a heart condition.. I asked for a pension for his mother who has been bereaved so deeply by the death of her child. Because she is a mother who has other children it does not follow that she did not suffer deeply when that child died. I was told that his death was not the result of his military service, and that it had nothing to do with it. Welt, if it had nothing to do with his service, your name, sir, is not Mr. Speaker and mine is not Jean Francois Pouliot. It is incredible. It is stamped with cruelty just as is the face of the man who was the chairman of the board and who took upon himself the tremendous responsibility to strike out the report of the heart specialist. The mother is entitled to a pension, and I send my whole file to the parliamentary assistant to the minister and ask him to have the case reviewed. I want a pension for the mother, and if I do not get it I will speak on each bill until the mother gets it, but I know I shall not have to do that, because it is a big file like a book. I know that I shall not have to do that because I do not speak to deaf ears, but it is something incredible.
There is something else; there is the distinction which has been made between those who followed the law strictly and those who have enlisted. Can you blame a man for following the law and abiding by it? Take a man who is a draftee, and who has been called a zombie. The law called upon him to report to a medical examiner, and then to the registrar. Then, if he had no cause for exemption, he had to report to the camp to follow the instructions of his commanding officer. He did all that, but he is looked upon as an untouchable of India. He is a despicable man because he did not enlist. It was so bad that even the man who followed the instructions of his commanding officer over the seas on the continent, and who did very well there, was not entitled to the military preference of the civil service because he had not signed a paper. Because he did not sign for overseas he was disbarred from preference. Happily I got in touch with the deputy minister of national defence and had it corrected, and that man was put in a position to enjoy the military preference just the same as the other boys in the army. Military preference has been so stupidly considered that even a sick man who enlisted, a man who knew that he was unfit, that he would be
rejected, is on the honour roll as one who served his country, although he enlisted only to be discharged. That is the difference. It is absurd. And those men who have enlisted for overseas are not entitled to gratuities. Here is a letter which was written by Mr. McTaggart, assistant director of reestablishment credit:
We wish to acknowledge receipt of your letter dated July 14 in regard to your entitlement to war service gratuity.
In the War Service Grants Act the definition of service is and we quote "while enlisted or obligated to serve without territorial limitation." It has been confirmed from your file that you were enrolled under the National Resources Mobilization Act and, therefore, you are not qualified by having been enlisted; your file also reveals that your entire service took place in Canada and, therefore, since you did not in fact leave the country, there is no question of your haying been "obligated to serve without territorial limitation."
I did not have time to read the whole bill, but when a man abides by the law he is entitled to the consideration given all good citizens. If the law was made in that way, they were not responsible for it. They obeyed the law, and now there is a difference in the treatment of those who followed both the spirit and the letter of the law and those who signed a paper. How many of the brass hats made Cook's tours over there just in order to qualify for the preference given in respect of overseas service? How many are there in the Department of National Defence who have never been in any theatre of war? Not so long ago I had a list of 280 officers, brass hats of the Department of National Defence, to say nothing of the N.C.O.'s and men, who had never been in any theatre of war but who were sending others over there. What a shame! But these men have received promotions, and they have been given efficiency medals.
There is something else I want to say. With the assistance of the minister, the assistance of his parliamentary assistant, to whom I wish good luck in whatever field he decides to carry on his activities, and the assistance of Brigadier Melville, to whom I want to give the benefit of the doubt and treat just as generously as I can, I hope something will be done to correct the injustices of the past and redress all wrongs. This morning I said Canada was generous to outsiders. That is true. At the present time we complain about the scarcity of lumber; we complain about the scarcity of food, and at the same time we keep men in the clink because they believed what had been said in this house by the Prime Minister, that the farmers were to be exempt from military service. Those men are in the
Pension Act

clink now, and some of them are in gaol. Those connected with the air force are in Bordeaux gaol, in Montreal, and they are handicapped as a result.
We are now discussing the pensions that are to be given. I am ready to give pensions to those who deserve them; I shall not kick about them; but, on the other hand, I think it is time to consider the war as a thing of the past and to look at the future in a different way from what has been the case up to the present. Those who 'have run the Department of National Defence, those who have been the power behind the throne in that department, are jingoists without war records. Those who have been in theatres of war, during either the first or second great wars, are more lenient. They have a broader outlook and are ready to act as civilized human beings. The others know very well they will be out on the street as soon as the army is demobilized; there will be no more soft jobs for them, so that they exercise their cruelty against honest citizens who deserve better treatment. If you are not satisfied that what I have said is the truth, Mr. Speaker, I can give the names of all those parasites who would be on the streets to-morrow if the clinks were closed. They are in the department; they are important; they travel like Xerxes when he crossed the Hellespont. One must admire them in their smart uniforms; they think they are masters of the land. I not believe members of the House of Commons are precisely -masters of the land, but they could easily be the masters of parliament if they ever felt like it. It is time to close the clinks. Why is it necessary to follow the example of the Meighen government, which was so unpopular that it was rejected by the people and Meighen could not be elected afterwards? Why follow that example? Well, there is a very good reason. It is that those who rule now in the Department of National Defence are exactly those who ruled when Meighen was in power, and it is those -men we have to fire at once.
There is one thing more I want to say before closing. It is that we are more united in misery than in happiness. At the present time, on the shoulders of everyone there is a heavy burden of taxation. It -makes us all feel more like brothers, and we should not be discouraged as to the future. But I hope that out of misery may come good understanding among Canadian citizens, and the example should be given by members of this house, who should come to a common understanding on main issues and decide them according to their good judgment and their patriotism. If I did not -believe sincerely and 
deeply in the good will, honesty, good purpose and patriotism of my colleagues I would not have come -back from God's country, especially at this time of year, to perform a necessary duty as a member of parliament. There is a ray of hope, and that ray of hope exists because of an event which has more importance than any legislation, an event of -more importance in the constitutional life of Canada than any statute of Westminster. I refer to the debate and discussion that took place on the Canada day bill. The matter is of minor importance. Whether it be called confederation day, national day, Canada day, Dominion day or anything else, I do not attach much importance to it; but on that occasion members of the House of Commons united to show that they were conscious of their responsibility, and that they wanted to do something. It was in connection with a minor issue. I hope this will occur each time a major issue arises in parliament; that members of parliament will unite, leaving aside all party considerations to do what they honestly think is good and right and in the interests of the country at large.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with much of what was said by the honourable and amiable member for Temis-couat-a (Mr. Pouliot) I am in agreement, particularly his remarks dealing with the pre-enlistment disabilities of veterans and their treatment when they apply for pension. However, like the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), I believe those matters were pretty thoroughly discussed in committee, and I do not propose to take the time of the house in going through all the discussions we carried on there.
It was my good fortune, along with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay), the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald) and the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Moore), all new members, to be placed on the veterans committee. Two of the senior members of our group, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), were also members and were able to give us guidance. Like the hon. member for Ro3fal (Mr. Brooks), I want to say that we enjoyed our association with the chairman. We did not have any really pitched battles. I expected there would be more in the way of political discussion, but there was much less than I expected. As has been mentioned, the chairman did not blow up, but once or twice I would1 not have been surprised if several people had blown up. However, we got over those difficulties with a minimum of partisanship. I believe this was due to the fact that every one, in spite of

Pension Act
what other ideas he may have had, was sincerely interested in trying to see what could be done for the veteran. On certain occasions the genial Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) honoured us with his presence. Occasionally he told us that there were certain points the government refused to accept, but that was the responsibility of the government. The committee could do nothing but accept those statements.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata when he said that officialdom is to blame. I think the officials of the department will do what the government tells them to do. We are hoping that some day the government will tell them to do some of the things that up to date they have not been told to do.
What I rose mainly to say on behalf of the party I represent was that so far as the pension bill is concerned we feel that we have had our part in the debate in the committee. A bill is now before us, having come from the committee, and the legislation will operate in its present form until further amendments are made. In the main we are prepared to watch the operations under this measure and be guided by the experience we gain. When we assemble at the next session we may make suggestions for amendments in the light of the experience we have gained by that time. It is doubtful if any new argument could be advanced, and we feel that that is probably the wisest course to take.
We hope that when parliament reassembles the veterans committee will again be set up. However, I remember one time when the Minister of Veterans Affairs was before the committee and the tension was pretty tight, he expressed the hope that never again would he have to have such a committee to deal with. But that was only on one occasion, and we hope that the committee will be reestablished at the next session so that we shall have an opportunity to make recommendations in the light of the experience we shall have gained. At that time some further appeals may 'be made by this group. I believe one member of this group has a certain definite matter regarding pensions to bring up, and I shall not take any further time because I am under threat of being shot if I speak for more than ten minutes.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member o'f the veterans committee I should like to join other hon. members in complimenting the chairman upon the way he filled his position. There were times when the debate waxed decidedly acrimonious; but, so far as I remember, on only one occasion did he find it necessary to
call on the deputy chairman to take his place while he let off a little steam. I believe this committee did a good job and has justified the amount of time that it has taken in its deliberations. On the other hand, it is perhaps unfortunate that the government has found it necessary to turn down some of the important recommendations of the committee, thereby nullifying some of the work that was done.
When the veterans committee was set up in 1945 there existed three main objections to the Pension Act. First, the insurance principle had been destroyed!; second, pensions were being denied on the ground that the disability was of pre-enlistment origin and, third, there existed a dead-line of April, 1944, in connection with marriages. By the time the committee had revised a draft of a proposed pension bill all these objections had been removed. Had the government seen fit to accept the draft bill in its amended form, I think we would have had a Pension Act of which we could have been proud. Unfortunately the government found it necessary to refuse to accept our amendments in regard: to the question of pre-enlistment origin and the deadline for marriages.
I should like to deal first with the insurance principle. I heard a few Liberals praise the government for having reinstated the insurance principle. This was done at the very commencement of the deliberations on the Pension Aot. Hon. members should, however, remember that it was the Liberal government that destroyed the insurance principle in May, 1940, by order in council.
If I remember rightly that was done largely as a result of a recommendation by the Minister of Finance. As a consequence several thousand veterans were deprived of pensions during the war and something in the neighbourhood of 200 widows were denied pensions.
A number of the members of the veterans committee which sat in 1940 tried to have the insurance principle reinstated, but the government of that day was not prepared to accede. There was a compromise to the extent of accepting the insurance principle in connection with veterans who were found to be in necessitous circumstances. I think it is important to remember that, while the insurance principle has now been restored, the payment of pensions will start only as of June 1, 1946, and as a consequence several thousand pensioners will have been without pension from the time the insurance principle was destroyed until June, 1946. But certainly I am pleased that the government saw fit to restore the insurance principle even at this late day.
Pension Act

The next point I should like to take up is the question of pensions being denied on the ground that disability was of pre-enlistment origin. The committee discussed this matter at great length. I think veterans have always felt that when a man was medically examined upon enlistment and declared to be in A-l condition, then if he were found to be medically unfit after several months or years of service, no attempt should be made to rule that his disability was of pre-enlistment origin. I think that was quite generally the opinion of the veterans committee. The committee proposed that a man's condition as recorded on his medical sheet at the time of enlistment should be presumed to be his true condition, unless it were found that some disability had been recorded on an examination prior to his enlistment. That amendment was carried; but unfortunately the minister declared, on behalf of the government, that they could not accept it; the bill we now have before us does not contain that amendment and the objectionable feature still remains in the act.
My last point concerns the dead-line for marriages of pensioners. If a pensioner marries after April 1, 1944, no increase is made in his pension because of the change in his status from a single to a married person, and no allowance can be made for children born of such a union. In the event of his death no pension can be paid to his widow. The committee voted unanimously to strike out that dead-line. But again, unfortunately, the government through the minister of pensions refused to accept that amendment, so that the bill before us contains the dead-line of April 1, 1944. The committee I think felt strongly on that question. It is not a big question so far as the money involved is concerned. The cost to the government would not be great to wipe out that dead-line. Today we all consider that it would be to the benefit of Canada to have an increase in population, and no doubt in the not distant future we shall be spending millions of dollars to bring people into this country. I would say that the very best way to expand our population is with Canadian-born children, and what better children could one have than children of veterans? Therefore I cannot understand why the government should discriminate against the old veterans by saying that any children born after a certain date not be recognized so far as pensions are concerned. I hope that, even at this late day, when we get to the section the government may see fit to take that dead-line out of this measure.

Apart from those two points, the dead-line for marriage, and disability of pre-enlistment origin, we in this group are pretty well behind the Pensions Act as it is now before us. But when the appropriate sections come up we shall no doubt have a few words to say on these two particular matters.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, within the last year thousands of our finest young men and women have come back to their homeland from the fighting fronts. Fortunately the majority of them have come back fit, and able to take their place in civilian life. But many have come back disabled. They have been handicapped for life by the service they have rendered to their fellow-Canadians. Many more, fortunately not as many as in the last war, but still many, many thousands of young Canadians who went overseas, will not come back. They are our war dead. But they leave here in Canada to mourn them their dependents and their other loved ones; and these loved ones of our young Canadians who will not come back, are the people in this country who know the real cost of war.
I suggest to this house that our feelings toward these young men and women who have come back and to the dependents of those who do not come back should b.e feelings of admiration and also of gratitude. That should be our approach when we discuss the problems having to do with them. The prime ministers of the empire put it very clearly away back in May of 1944, when at the end of their historic conference in London they issued a statement which contained this sentence:
To all our armed forces who in many lands are preserving our liberty with their lives we express our admiration and gratitude.
That was before D-day, before our troops had landed on the continent of Europe. But we should still have that feeling. We should be filled with admiration and gratitude.
We are under two great obligations. The first is to see that the young people who have come back are absorbed into the life of the nation. The second is that those who are disabled and the dependents of the fallen should be compensated generously for the sacrifices they have made. I do not think there is one member of this house who would disagree with my statement of those two great obligations under which we stand at this present time.
But, Mr. Speaker, it is not only a question of being under these obligations at this time. It is comparatively easy to remember them now, with the war over such a short time ago. But these are obligations that will continue

Pension Act
year in and year out until the last disabled Canadian and the last dependent of a Canadian who did not come back, have passed on. For so long will these obligations remain on the Canadian people. And I make bold to state to-day that these obligations will not be met by any so-called Veterans Charter-of 1946.
The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) has pointed out that these veterans bills that are to be considered by the house are but one step. They are the legislation which we believe should be enacted at this time. Personally I think it is a great mistake to refer to them as constituting a Veterans Charter. It sounds very nice. It brings a certain amount of credit to those of us on the committee, who really have worked hard and in a fine spirit to see that these bills are the very best that could be written. But the danger is this, that the Canadian people will say: "Oh, well, now that we have written a Veterans Charter we have done what should be done for the veterans; so let us get on with some other business." For that reason I think it was unwise to term these bills a Veterans Charter. I am not questioning the motive in using those words as a title for the bills, but it would have been wiser not to try to spread the impression abroad throughout the land that we are now preparing a great Veterans Charter.
You see, Mr. Speaker, there will be improvements required every year. There are improvements required at this very moment in this Pension Act, which is the bill now being considered. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has referred to some defects in the bill. I shall deal to-day with only one, which I urge upon the minister should be remedied before the bill becomes law.
There is no provision in this pension bill for the veteran who has been discharged as medically unfit but yet cannot qualify for pension because of a ruling made by the pension commission -that his disability arose from a pre-enlistmen-t condition. This applies not only to men who served in Canada but also to the young Canadians who served overseas. We were given figures as of December 31, 1945, by the chairman of the pension commission, showing that there were 7,810 young Canadians who were fit enough to be enlisted in the forces and taken overseas, who eventually were brought back and discharged as medically unfit and yet were not granted any pension entitlement because of a pre-enlistment condition. They were not even granted anything for aggravation by service. I repeat that figure-7,810.
The figure for those who served only in Canada was 54,207. That number of young Canadians enlisted in the forces, served in Canada only, were discharged as medically unfit, and yet were not entitled to any pension either for original disability or for aggravation, because they were said to have a preenlistment condition.
There is something wrong there either with the law or with the doctors. All these men were carefully examined, far more carefully examined in this war than those of us were who served in the last war. We, or some of us, "got by" on nearly anything. In this war there was the most careful examination. Yet we find that, after men have been examined and enrolled, and have served for years, another doctor discharges them as medically unfit, and a third group of doctors, working under the pension commission, say, "Well, they had a pre-enlistment condition; presumably they were sick before they ever got in the army, or they were going to'be sick anyway, and that is that, and they are not entitled to any pension." These men are being ruled out or, in some cases, granted only a partial pension, on the ground that the condition originated before enlistment.
Mr. Speaker, that is an injustice which should be remedied, and it should be remedied in this bill. I believe that could be done by inserting in the Pension Act a new provision to this general effect-I am not giving the exact wording-which I think should be covered by a new section of the act:
That there shall be a presumption that a man's condition as recorded on admission to service was in fact his condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration was due to his service.
In other words, it shall be presumed that if he was enrolled as fit he was actually fit, and that if, during his service, his physical condition deteriorates the state must show that such deterioration was not due to his service; otherwise he would be entitled to some pension.
That suggestion was made before the special committee. As the hon. member for Acadia has said, it was considered at some length, and finally, on motion of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), an amendment to the act was recommended. Hon. members will find it in the proceedings of the committee on May 31, 1946. The hon. member for Nanaimo moved that there be put in the act a new section reading as follows:
62A. There shall be a presumption that an applicant's condition as recorded on his acceptance as a member of the forces was in fact his
Pension Act

condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration during service was due to such service.
Then, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), a proviso was added, worded as follows: subject to the provisions of paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 111 of this act.
That proviso covers the case where a man's condition was obvious on his admission to the service; in other words, if he had a wooden leg and had been able to get by the doctor even with that wooden leg! Or where he had wilfully concealed his condition, or where his condition had been recorded on another medical examination, say a civilian medical examination, prior to his enlistment. That amendment was adopted unanimously by the special committee on veterans affairs.
But then the government came in, a week later, and said, "We are not willing to accept that amendment." I think the reason they did so was that the pension commission did not like it. The minister showed no particular antagonism to the amendment; I believe he would have been willing to let it go into the bill. That was on June 7, and after we had passed all the sections of a draft bill. I moved that the draft bill be reported to the house, but the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) moved an amendment, and later on the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) moved other amendments, the effect of which was to change that draft bill into the form that the government wanted. So that the bill as it comes before the house to-day is not the bill which was really recommended by the members of the veterans committee when they were considering it section by section.
The change made in regard to this preenlistment condition was that the new section was struck out, and to take its place two words were added to what is known as "the benefit of the doubt" section, section 62. The words added were "and presumptions", and putting them in section 62 meant nothing at all. So I repeat my suggestion to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) that, when this bill goes into committee, he allow it to be amended to include a new section, and I intend to move such a section, No. 63A-there has been some change in the numbering-to this effect:
63A. In respect of an application for entitlement to pension arising out of world war II there shall be a presumption that the condition of the member of the forces as recorded on his acceptance was in fact his condition at that time and that any subsequent deterioration during service was due to such service; subject to the provisos contained in paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 11 of this act.

I will give the minister a copy of the proposed change when I am through.
Another improvement which could be made at this time, without waiting until next year, is to give the dependents' board of trustees power to help out the family of a veteran. As hon. members know, that board was set up under the Department of National Defence- it is not under the Department of Veterans Affairs at all, even at the present time-and was provided with funds so that the case of a needy family could be met. The board has done splendid work. I know that in the city of Vancouver many families have been helped in that way who otherwise would have had no helping hand at all. I suggest to the house that for the next year or two that dependents' board of trustees be provided with funds to help the families of veterans; for example, the family of a veteran who cannot qualify Tor pension and yet in whose family there will be great suffering without such assistance. The board would not have to carry on indefinitely; it is simply a suggestion for the immediate post-war period.
When I opened my speech this afternoon I mentioned that we had an obligation to absorb these young men and women into the life of the nation. I do not intend to go very far along that line to-day because there are other bills which deal with that obligation. But there are two matters which will not come up under other bills; they are contained in the recommendations which have been made by the committee. The first has to do with the civil service preference. The committee recommended in its final report:
That the present civil service preference for disabled veterans and veterans who served overseas be extended to cover all employment, both temporary and permanent, by the House of Commons-
That means by us, right here; it means on our own front doorstep.
-and by dominion government agencies inclusive of crown companies.
The civil service preference at the present time applies only to those who come under the Civil Service Act. The Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) can correct me, but I should think that would be perhaps only half or two-thirds of the total number of civil servants. In any event, there are thousands of government positions that are not subject to the veteran's preference. I suggest that, without further delay, provision should be made by the government to extend the preference to all dominion government agencies, including these new crown companies that are being set up.
The importance of such a move is that people on the outside, ordinary businessmen,

Pension Act
will follow the example set by the government. If the government has a crown company which does not give preference to veterans, then the man doing business with that company, or who knows of its activities, will say, "Why do I have to give a preference to veterans when this government company is not giving it?" And provincial governments are apt to do the same. They will say, "The dominion government does not give a preference. These men served1 under the dominion and the dominion will not give them a preference; why should we?" It weakens the position of the veteran all across Canada, and therefore I appeal to the government to take action to extend this preference, and to take that action quickly.
The other recommendation of the committee to which I would refer is the following:
That the government consider the extension of priorities in the purchase of surplus war assets to veterans on certification by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Just within the last day or two another department of government, the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, has said that there is to be no more preference to veterans in the purchase of cars and trucks because you cannot trust them-they will go and make a deal with some civilian and there will be a lot of under-the-table business carried on. Therefore the priority must go.
That is not good enough. The committee on veterans affairs went into the whole question carefully. We say that where a veteran needs a truck or a car in order to become reestablished, and gets a certificate from the veterans affairs department that such is the case, then he should receive priority; and I would urge the government to see that a change is made along that line.
In conclusion, I have dealt to-day primarily with the Pension Act; with the men and women who have been disabled and the dependents of those who have not come back. This house was elected in June, 1945, just a little over a year ago, when Canada was still at war in the Pacific, it is true, but the fighting in Europe had ended and it was obvious that Japan could not hold out longer. Every member elected to this house knew, and the Canadian people knew, that to this House of Commons would be entrusted the writing of laws to protect those who had been disabled, and the dependents of the fallen; and no matter what the members of the house do, no matter what the Canadian people do, they can never adequately repay their fellow Canadians who have suffered. But a genuine
attempt to do so should be our first concern, not only in this post-war session, but throughout the whole life of the present parliament.

I have listened this afternoon with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green); and, while Listening to those remarks, I was thinking of the last session of parliament, prior to prorogation, when the report of the veterans committee was presented to the house. If I remember rightly, there was little discussion of. or comment on the report because we felt in the house that that committee had done its work thoroughly and well and that the country generally was in favour of being generous to those who had served Canada so splendidly in its wars.
Now again, through this session, a committee of the house has been studying veterans affairs, and again its report is coming before the house in the form of the present bills.
I have not had the privilege of serving- on that committee, although I was a veteran of the first great war, but I discovered that even if I had been a member of the committee I would not have been permitted to bring individual cases on the floor of the committee. Those have been ruled out, and it seems to me that this is the place where some individual cases should be dealt with when we are considering the principles of the pension bill.
The first case I wish to refer to is that of a Canadian soldier, at least a soldier who fought for Canada in the great war of 1914-18, who was severely wounded in that war and was subsequently pensioned for his disability. Later on, when he tried to go out and do a little for himself to add to his pension, it was agreeable to the pension commission that he should do so, and a promise was made that if he found he could not get along his pension would be reinstated to its original sum. In the meantime, this young man goes down to live in the United States and then discovers that originally he was a United States citizen. He has not had his pension reinstated to its original sum, and in spite of all his appeals he has been turned down. I have taken the matter up with the pension commission, and they inform me that there are fourteen or fifteen bulky files dealing with this particular case. I am not concerned about how many files they have; if an injustice has been done to a soldier who fought for Canada, the matter of the number of files should not enter into the case.
Pension Act

Second, the immigration officials refused to allow this man to come to Canada. All he asks is that he be allowed to come to Canada, go before a medical board and have a rediagnosis of his case. "Oh, no",.they said, "we cannot let this man into Canada at all. He is not a Canadian citizen and if we did let him in he is liable to become a public charge on Canada."
When a man is willing to hazard his life and fight for Canada and to be wounded in that service, to my mind such treatment is hardly good enough. Although the pension commission may say it is a closed case; although the immigration officials may say they will not let this man come in, I still feel there is one man who in his breast has a rankling sense of injustice against Canada. To-day all that he asks is to be given a square deal.

The second case that I wish to deal with is that of a man from my own constituency. This man enlisted in Cranbrook on June 13, 1940. Two days later he was placed on a troop train bound for Vancouver. While he was travelling on the train, he suffered an accident, a stone came rolling down the mountainside, smashed through the car window and struck the man on the head. As a result of these injuries, he is suffering from a nervous condition, defective hearing in the left ear with perforation of the eardrum, and defective vision of the left eye. This man has been discharged without a pension. When he went before the appeal board of the Canadian pension commission on June 19, 1942, his case was outlawed. He was told that he was suffering from pre-enlistment conditions. I should like to read for the record a statement made by the doctor who examined this man when he enlisted and when he was discharged. It reads as follows:
Cranbrook, British Columbia, April 16, 1941.
To whom it may concern:
To those interested, I examined this man when he enlisted, and according to the records which we have there was nothing to show that this man had any of the following:
1.	Nervous condition.
2.	Defective hearing, left ear with perforated eardrum.
3.	Defective vision, left eye.
The above are conditions for which this man was discharged from the army. I feel that these conditions are largely due to the accident which occurred while this man was en route to the coast from Cranbrook.
Signed Melville J. Swartz, M.D.

speechtext: I do not want to speak on this question, but I shall make an observation. Every hon. member knows that the commission has full jurisdiction in these matters. The minister has no right to overrule the commission; it has full jurisdiction. To try to get a suggestion from the minister that he will overrule the commission is asking him to assume something which parliament has denied him. I urge the hon. member not to bring up individual cases in this discussion. Every hon. member knows that they have dozens of cases which have been brought to their attention. If the hon. member brings up individual cases there will be the feeling that other hon. members should do the same thing. I say this as a matter of getting the bill through without having these cases threshed out on the floor of the house where there is no power to deal with them. Because of that, I ask the hon. member not to press these individual cases.

speechtext: I rise to a point of order. I suggest to the hon. member who has just spoken that it is always the privilege of any hon. member of parliament to bring before the house anything which his conscience tells him should be brought up there.
