speechtext: A few moments ago I brought to the attention of the house a case in which I am very much interested. The Minister of Veterans Affairs intimated that he has the file, which he would be pleased to show me. I want to accept his invitation, and to tell the minister I shall be glad to see it at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: In the meantime, I know the man; and- I know that once the crown has sued the Canadian Pacific Railway Company because of injuries sustained by a soldier in the crown's service and has accepted the sum of S300 from that company in settlement, because that is the answer given to a question which was placed on the order paper, then the crown must accept some responsibility to the soldier who was injured. If I know anything at all of logic that holds true.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I wish my hon. friend would reserve judgment until he reads the file and finds out all the conditions surrounding the matter.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I think this man has a claim for a pension. Failing that, if his case cannot be reviewed by the pension commission, I want to ask here in this House of Commons for permission from the crown, through the Attorney General, to sue the crown on this man's behalf.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, am I to understand that any man, I do'not care whether he is a member of parliament or a private individual, has the right to see any soldier's file; that some man who was afraid to fight for his country can go and see the file of a man who did fight?

speechtext:
I
want to object to that phrase, "a man who is afraid to fight for his country." I shall not accept it as applying to any constituent of mine. This man enlisted in His Majesty's service.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: If you will sit down you will find out that I am not referring to your man at all. I am merely asking if any private individual or -anyone else has the right to see a soldier's file. I think the leader of your party will agree with the point I am bringing up. Do not sound off until you understand what it is all about. Has any individual the right to see a soldier's file.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: The Minister of Veterans Affairs made that proposal to the hon. member.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I do not think the minister had any rignt to do so.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Oh, yes; the minister has every right in a case like this. Ordinarily the hon. member is quite correct; a soldier's file cannot be seen except with the permission of a minister of the crown.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Then may I ask another question? I presume that is in confidence, is it? In other words, if a member can ask the minister to see a file, and the minister shows it to- him, can he go to some political newspaper and give the contents of a man's private file to the public? I doubt it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Where there is deliberate misrepresentation in regard to conditions in any particular case, which imputes injustice to the department, the minister is entitled to show the file.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Well, I should like to ask another question. I am not disputing the minister's statement, but I am trying to protect the interests of the private soldier. I -think, if a man has committed deliberate misrepresentation it is the duty of the department to- prosecute him, rather than to pass around the information.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I am not yet clear as to what is to be done in this particular case in regard to which I am appealing to-day. Can it be reopened by the pension commission?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may answer the question- asked, by the hon. member

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I have not yet finished asking it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
The hon. member wants to know -what can be done. The law, the Pension Act, definitely provides what can be done. It definitely states that the pension commission has full jurisdiction in the matter, the same as any court of law, and that it must interpret the facts and the law. That is in the

Pension Act
statute. When the commission comes to a decision, neither the minister nor this house has any right to interfere with its jurisdiction. That right has been conferred upon the commission, and I am sure no soldier organization would want to change the law so that the judgment of the commission could be interfered with by any member of parliament or any member of the government. When the hon. member asks whether the minister will undertake to interfere with the jurisdiction of the pension commission, the answer must be that he has no right to do so, under a statute of this country. Surely that is an answer to the hon. member.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: But it does not prevent a member of this house from rising in his place and airing what he considers to be an injustice. I should like to say something with regard to the file. I agree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley, but I think, when a member of parliament is invited to see a soldier's file, that member is placed upon his honour to exercise his responsibility.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: I agree.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
That is always done, as far as 'I know.
Mr. BLiACKMORE: Unless a member has a right to look at a file, how can he bring an injustice to the attention of the house?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
I was going to say that every hon. member who has had anything to do with the pension commission knows that its chairman is ready to go to almost any lengths to discuss any case which any hon. member thinks has not been dealt with fairly or justly. I have never known a public servant more anxious to go into all the facts in order to satisfy a member of parliament that justice has been done. Instead) of discussing this matter on the floor of the house, where hundreds of other cases might just as properly be brought up, which would delay the passing of this legislation, I would appeal to the hon. member to take his case to the chairman of the pension commission.. There I guarantee that the file will be laid before him, and when he looks at the file and has a chance to see both sides I am sure he will be fully satisfied. I ask him to take up the matter with the board that has jurisdiction, instead of bringing it up on the floor of this house. The hon. gentleman mentioned another hon. member. If the hon. gentleman presents individual cases, I know of others which may be brought up by other hon. members; and if each hon. gentleman exercises the right which
the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says is the right of his colleague-, we may as well resign ourselves to the fact that this single bill will take up at least two weeks.
I make this appeal for this reason. We had wonderful cooperation in the committee, and our desire was to try to get this legislation through within a reasonable time. The hope was that anything about which we could not do anything in this parliament would not be discussed at any length at this time. Of course the hon. member is not bound by that understanding, but I suggest to him that the representative of his party on the steering committee entirely agreed with that attitude and, I know, is anxious that it should be carried out, in order to get this legislation through in the interests of the soldiers.

subtopic: ENLARGEMENT OF SCOPE AND APPLICATION-REORGANIZATION OF COMMISSION
speechtext: May I rise on a point of order? As a -member who has been in the house f-or nearly eleven years, I am interested in the point raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I think that is a pretty important point; and I do not believe the solution is that which has been suggested by the minister or by those who have spoken. I do not think any member of the government or any member of parliament would stand for a moment for any ordinary, private member of the house snooping in the files of -men who have served overseas, or given any other service. But that is not the point. In each of these cases where files have been opened to a private member of the house, I believe it has always been done under this circumstance, which I think must be -borne in mind; that is, that the man asking for the privilege of looking at the file is in a sense the agen-t of the man whose file it is. I do not think I have any right to go to a man's file unless I am representing him; I do not think I have any right to go into somebody else's file just to find out something, even though I am a member of parliament. However, I think there is perfect justification-, for the hon. member for Kootenay East for instance, who is putting forward a man's case, to go to that man's file. The minister should feel at liberty to open up that file, because there is no question then of confidentiality being offended in any way, shape or form.
